Childish
CHILD-ish
adj. (belonging to a child; and so immature where maturity is owed)
From child with the adjectival ending. The Authorized Version uses it once, in Paul's account of the difference between what he was and what he became: when I became a man, I put away childish things.

Biblical Definition

When I was a child, I spake as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child: but when I became a man, I put away childish things. The verse sits inside the chapter on charity, and it is an argument about the present age. Paul has just said that prophecies shall fail, tongues shall cease, knowledge shall vanish away, for we know in part and we prophesy in part; but when that which is perfect is come, then that which is in part shall be done away. Childhood is his figure for now, and manhood for then, and the next verse completes it: for now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face. The dictionary therefore takes the verse as eschatology before it is ethics, and only then as ethics. Where Scripture does apply childishness morally it is careful about which direction: Brethren, be not children in understanding: howbeit in malice be ye children, but in understanding be men. Innocence of malice is to be kept and the thinking is to grow up. Ephesians names the danger of failing to: that we henceforth be no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): belonging to a child; trifling; puerile; ignorant; silly; in Scripture, what a man puts away on becoming a man.

expand to see more

CHILDISH, a. Belonging to a child; trifling; puerile.

CHILDISH, a. Ignorant; silly; weak; not becoming a man.

PUERILE, a. Boyish; juvenile; trifling; as puerile amusements.

MATURITY, n. A state of ripeness; completion; the state of being complete, perfect or finished.

UNDERSTANDING, n. The faculty of the human mind by which it apprehends the real state of things.

Key Scripture

1Co 13:11 — "When I was a child, I spake as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child: but when I became a man, I put away childish things."

1Co 13:12 — "For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known."

1Co 14:20 — "Brethren, be not children in understanding: howbeit in malice be ye children, but in understanding be men."

Eph 4:14 — "That we henceforth be no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive;"

Modern Corruption

Doctrinal seriousness is treated as a hardening that maturity should soften, and simplicity of faith is confused with simplicity of mind; Paul commands the opposite, that Christians be children in malice and men in understanding.

expand to see more

1 Corinthians 14:20 separates two things the church habitually confuses. In malice be ye children — keep the incapacity for spite, the absence of grudge-keeping, the artlessness. In understanding be men — grow up in doctrine, in judgment, in the ability to weigh a claim. The common failure inverts both: congregations sophisticated in suspicion and infantile in theology. Hebrews rebukes exactly that in people who ought to have been teachers and still needed milk, and says that strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age, even those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil.

Ephesians names what immaturity costs. Children are tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive. The remedy Paul gives is not less doctrine but more, delivered by pastors and teachers, until we all come in the unity of the faith, and of the knowledge of the Son of God, unto a perfect man. And the manner is fixed in the same paragraph so that the growing up never becomes contempt: speaking the truth in love.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek nepios (G3516), an infant, a child, one without speech; teleios (G5046), complete, full-grown; katargeo (G2673), to put away or render inoperative.

expand to see more

Greek nepios (G3516) — an infant, a babe, and so childish; when I was a child.

Greek teleios (G5046) — complete, mature, full-grown; that which is perfect.

Greek katargeo (G2673) — to render idle, to abolish, to put away; I put away childish things.

Greek kakia (G2549) — malice, badness; in malice be ye children.

Greek kludonizomai (G2831) — to be tossed by waves; tossed to and fro.

Usage

"“when I became a man, I put away childish things” — the single occurrence."

"“in malice be ye children, but in understanding be men” — the two directions."

"“tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine” — the cost of not growing."
